speechtext:
Last Thursday I gave notice that I would propose to-day that the standing orders of the house be amended by inserting the following:
9(a). Upon a division a member is not obliged to vote.
In moving this amendment I do not propose anything new. I simply desire to clarify the situation and to enable the house and yourself, sir, as guardian of the rules of this house, to avoid a repetition of the little embroilment of last week. That, however, I regard, as a matter of fact, only as an incident. What I wish to make clear is that there never has been and that there is not at the present time any standing order or set rule governing the manner in which members must vote or refrain from voting. What has -been quoted in this house or outside the house as Rule 68 is not and never has been a rule; it is one of the footnotes which Mr. Beauchesne has incorporated as comments upon the very rule
which I propose to discuss to-day-that is, standing order No. 9. And even at that, Mr. Beauchesne's footnote, No. 68, which my good friend from Charlevoix-fiaguenay (Mr. Casgrain) mistook for a rule of the house, is but the reproduction of a paragraph of Bourinot's fourth edition, at page 381, as any man familiar with Mr. Beauchene's book, or with the rules of the house, can easily find out; because there, after paragraph 68, you have "B-381." Besides, that paragraph in Bourinot's fourth edition of 1916, which was edited by a predecessor of our able clerk, Doctor Flint, is also a verbatim reproduction of the same words used by Sir John Bourinot in the first edition of his book in 1884, at page 389. Now, that comment of Sir John Bourinot, reproduced as it has been from time to time, was absolutely true and accurate as applied to the practices of the British and Canadian houses in 1884. I do not think I shall have any trouble in demonstrating that it is no longer applicable to the rules of this house as they were revised in 1927.
Now to give a short history of our standing orders. The first set of rules or standing orders of this house were adopted on December 20, 1867, as may be found in the Journals of the House of Commons for the year 1867-68, at pages 115 to 125. Neither in these standing orders, any more than in any other standing orders following, nor in the present standing orders, was there any disposition regarding the right of members either to vote or not to vote. But there was a general governing clause, adopted as standing order No. 116, which stated:
In all unprovided cases the Rules, Usages and Forms of the House of Commons of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland shall be followed.
That is what I call the governing rule of all our standing orders, from that day until the present time. As it was in 1867, that general clause did not make any mention as to date with regard to the usages pursued in the House of Commons in England; they were to apply from time to time. The first time that the matter was brought up in the house-at least the first time, and I think it is sufficient, that I have discovered-was in 1879, when the house voted, if I remember rightly, on the famous legislation concerning the Canadian Pacific Railway. An hon. member having voted, his vote was challenged by one of the ministers of the crown, Mr. Caron, because he had paired; upon which the Prime Minister, Sir John Macdonald, leader of the house, stood up and stated, in contradiction of his own colleague, that-

Rules-Members Not Voting
Every member in the house, if called upon, was compelled to vote, and even if a gentleman got up and stated that he had paired, the house could compel him to vote, because, if he had paired, he must leave the house before the Vote was taken. This was English practice.
If the rule stood now as it was then, it would mean that every time a vote is taken, members getting up and declaring that they have not voted because they are paired, break the same rule, or rather what has been mentioned as such, but which as a matter of fact is not a rule but only a practice. Let us see, however. Upon this opinion of Sir John Macdonald, implicitly endorsed by the whole house, Sir John Bourinot based the comment which I have quoted and which Mr. Beauchesne has reproduced in his paragraph, No. 68, misquoted as a rule of this house. The only rule was the practice as defined by Sir John Macdonald in 1879, then in force in England as here; because it must be noted that Sir John Macdonald invoked it as applying to this house inasmuch as it was the English practice.
In 1906, however, the British House of Commons revised its standing orders and adopted the following rule:	[DOT]
No. 29. A member may vote in a division although he did not hear the question put.
And paragraph 2:
A member is not obliged to vote.
-which are the exact words that I have put in the motion I now propose to the house. Now, did this apply to Canada? No. And why not? Because in 1906, the same year, in the month of March, the House of Commons of Canada had revised its rules and in substitution for the governing rule 116 of 1867 it had introduced a new governing clause. It is called "General Rule No. 1." This, I claim, is the most important of the standing orders because it governs the whole. It reads:
In ah eases not provided for hereinafter- That is, by the standing orders.
-or by sessional or other orders, the rules, usages and forms of proceeding of the House of Commons of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, in force on the first day of July 1867, shall be followed.
As Doctor Flint quotes in his posterior edition of Bourinot's work, the effect of this was to prevent the application to the House of Commons of Canada of the new standing order adopted in England in December 1906. So that when, in 1022', Mr. Beauchesne issued the first edition of his comments, he was perfectly justified in inserting this footnote. It was 'then under No. 69, now under No. 68. This paragraph says that an hon. member is Obliged to vote. That was copied, I repeat,

from feir John Bourinot. Then paragraph 70^69 of the second edition (1927)-reads as follows:
Under ancient custom, refusal to vote was considered a serious parliamentary offence, but the practice was changed in 1906 by the British house adopting a standing order whereby a member is not obliged to vote. That standing order does not apply to the Canadian Commons The practice has not been changed in Canada where every member who has heard the question put is bound to vote..
This is the second paragraph referred to by the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Cas-grain) as being another rule of the house. The hon. member was apparently under the misapprehension that Mr. Beauchesne is the parliament of Canada and that his comments are to be taken as rules of this house, just as a lawyer in consulting with a client might confuse the opinion of a commentator with the text of a statute or of a judgment delivered by the court. I do not think my hon. friend would act in that way in his capacity as a lawyer.
Mr. CA8GRAIN: Not all the time.

speechtext:
My hon. friend did not do it intentionally. I am sure that most hon. members of this house are apt to make such mistakes once in a while; and may I say for the benefit of the hon. lady member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) that many members of the press gallery seemed to be under the same misapprehension. Neither Sir John Bourinot nor Mr. Beauchesne is the parliament of Canada, nor should a private opinion expressed by even such eminent parliamentary jurists as Sir John Bourinot or Mr. Beauchesne prevail over the expressed will of parliament.
I think I can demonstrate quite easily that in 1927 this house changed its attitude with regard to this very question and adopted a new rule which put into effect the practice which for many years, even previous to 1906, had been in force in Great Britain. In 1927, as every hon. member knows, our rules were revised. Heaven knows-my hon. friend beside me (Mr. Neill) will support me in this- they were not revised with the idea of giving more freedom to independent members of this house. However, the committee which revised our rules did not think it necessary to impose upon hon. members the obligation of voting if conscientiously they did not feel like voting. What did they do? They introduced a new governing rule. While the House of Commons had, in 1006, declared that such practices, customs and usages of the House of Commons of the United Kingdom would apply here only as prior to 1867, under the

Rules-Members Not Voting
rules adopted by this house in 1927 we reverted to the principle of 1867, and in fact made it much clearer. The general rule governing all such cases now is standing order No. 1, which reads as follows:
In all cases not provided for hereinafter or by sessional or other orders, the usages and customs of the House of Commons of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland as in force at the time shall be followed so far as they may be applicable to this house.
The principle of applying only those rules in force in 1867 was deleted. So that from 1927 on, we have it stated in so many words in our standing orders, which are the laws governing the proceedings in this house, that the forms and practices now in force in England are in force here to govern all cases not provided for by our own standing orders. Under this new governing rule, which was a revolution, whether right or wrong, the then Speaker, Hon. Mr. Lemieux, decided twice during the session of 1928-the first session following the adoption of these rules-that a member although present in the house was not obliged to vote.
The first occasion occurred on March 27, 1928, to be found at page 1755 of the debates of that year. Curiously enough, the challenge was issued by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner), so he has good reason to know the rule which was applied at that time. The hon. member raised the point that the then Minister of Immigration, Mr. Forke, had not voted, and then followed a very picturesque and I think very true comment by the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin), as follows:
'The minister is not the only one who did not understand what he was voting for.
I think that is one of the best comments on parliamentary government ever made. Mr. Speaker Lemieux spoke thus:
The rule is that members who are present when a motion is read must vote if they are in the house whilst the division is being taken. But when an hon. member declares that he does not know what the amendment is about, he is excused from voting. That is the practice followed in the British House of Commons.
Unfortunately, the Speaker, who had given his decision on the spur of the moment, did not quote the authorities. However, on May 26 of the same year another occasion arose on which the then Minister of Finance, Mr. Robb, challenged the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) for abstaining from voting. The decision of the Speaker, which appears on page 3420 of the debates of that year, was as follows:
Generally, under the practice of the house, an hon. member who has heard the question put must vote. However, lately, since 1906,
I know, in the British parliament this time-honoured practice has been ignored; I have seen a standing order-
The one which I read a moment ago-
-to the effect that when a member does not feel justified in voting he need not do so. I decided this point some weeks ago, when the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Forke) was in the same position; he declared that because of conscientious reasons he did not think it wise to vote on the question.
The cause of the confusion which arose last week reduces itself to this:	In publishing his
book in 1927 our excellent clerk did not delete those so-called rules Nos. 68 and 69. They were not really rules, they were opinions previously expressed by Sir John Bourinot and Mr. Beauchesne. At the time they were expressed, they were quite proper but had no further application after the change of the governing rule made in 1927. In justice to our clerk, whom I consider to be one of the best parliamentary authorities, not only in Canada but in the British Empire, it must be said that this book was published a few weeks after the close of the session. He himself in his preface points out the fact that because of the changes adopted during the previous session he added some two hundred footnotes to the present edition, and struck out other footnotes which had no further application. His mistake would probably have been made by nine out of ten, if not by forty-nine out of fifty men. The clerk had to follow, and he did so with much industry and legal insight, the full effect of this new governing clause No. 1 upon all the standing orders and practices of this house. It would have taken months fully to realize what the effect of this new rule would be on the various practices and customs theretofore undefined either in the rules of our house or in those of the British house. So I repeat and I think I could end by saying that what I am moving to-day is in order to dispel a misapprehension, to put into concrete form what has been since 1927 the unwritten rule of the house and assented to by jurisprudence from the chair the year after the rules were revised.
But before I take my seat I want to go a little further, and I hope the house will acquit me of a desire simply to give a little satisfaction to my amour propre. What I want td demonstrate in my closing words is that this rule, as now written and applied in England-and it was applied in practice several years before it was enacted in their standing orders-is in strict conformity with

Rules-Members Not Voting
the evolution of parliamentary government that has taken place both in England and here, not to speak of other countries. I quite realize that for the many years during which the House of Commons was divided into two strictly regulated parties, the shepherds of those two flocks, for instance my good friends the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Casgrain) and the hon. member for West Algoma (Mr. Simpson), were mostly concerned with bringing in all the stranded ewes and making them vote in accordance with the party whip or order. But whether they like the situation or not, in England as here, with the extension of the suffrage not only to the various classes of men but to women as well, the point has been reached that the two party system is no longer satisfactory to a growing number of men and women either in Great Britain or in Canada. I find it quite legitimate on the part of the old party leaders, their followers and their press men, to deprecate that growth, but still it is there; and so long as there are fractions of the Canadian community, as in England, who send to parliament men who are not bound to follow the dictates of the two old parties, not only must those men be allowed freedom to express their opinions in concrete motions as they present them in contradistinction to the motions presented by the government or the official opposition; but in addition we must acknowledge to those men elected by the free electorate of Canada, the same liberty of not voting for any motion presented by a Conservative or by a Liberal if they find in that motion something to which they agree and something with which they disagree. Is that not reasonable?

speechtext: If this be the rule as it exists now, what is the necessity of enacting this new rule as would be done by the hon. member's motion?

maintopic: RULES OF THE HOUSE

speechtext:
This is simply to clarify the matter. First of all it was evident last week that many hon. members were misinformed as to the situation. I am quite sure and I am prepared to say that every one of them was in perfect good faith. Under what circumstances are laws or regulations passed in the British house? In such matters I always rely upon British practice because, after all, the practice of parliamentary government is essentially British, and whether we agree or disagree with many things in British policy, we must agree that the British parliament, as a parliament, remains the example. Why did they adopt that rule in England? Because the point had been reached when

first the Irish party, then the Labour party, and then the Independent Labour party, had cropped up; and very often they were not permitted to express their views otherwise than by abstention from voting. Very wisely here as in England we have stuck to the rule that we should not have numerous amendments. But suppose even we changed that so as to give to my friends to my left, the Progressives-and even they are now nearly divided into two groups-or my friends of the Labour group, or myself or my good neighbour, the right to express our views in subamendments. After those subamendments have been disposed of we are obliged to vote either for or against the amendment, or the motion, or to abstain from voting. I do not want to refer to a past debate, but as a matter of illustration I may say that I stated quite clearly that the amendment of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) suited me in one respect but not in another. By voting against it I would have been forced to deny something in which I believed and by voting for it I would have been forced to approve something I did not approve. It is evident it was under the weight of such considerations that the change was made in England and I ask the house to make the same change here simply to clarify the question.
May I appeal to both the leader of the government and the leader of the opposition for whom-and they know this although we may differ on many occasions,-I have the greatest respect? I appeal especially to the Prime Minister whose marvellous erudition in matters of law and of parliamentary government has many times given me wonder. He is undoubtedly one of the greatest legal minds in this country. I am quite sure he is sincerely very much concerned with the preservation of the best traditions of British government. May I remind him of this? When the change was made in England it was proposed by Sir Henry Campbell Bannerman, not an upsetter of things, I believe, one of the most respected of British statesmen in the last century. Around him sat as ministers of the crown such men as Sir Edward Grey, James Bryce-I call them as they were then styled, mere commoners but men of great value- Mr. Haldane, who later on became Chancellor of the Exchequer, and Mr. Asquith. On the other side the opposition was led in the house by Mr. Arthur Balfour, surrounded by such men as the Right Hon. Joseph Chamberlain, his son Austen, Lord Robert Cecil, and that veteran, not so well known perhaps outside of England but so much re-

Rides-Members Not Voting
spected in England, Sir Edward Clarke, who died just a few days ago, one of the shining lights and one of the most respected men in the British parliament as well as before the British courts. All those men sat there, and whilst many other proposals which were enacted then by a majority were discussed, this disposition which I ask the Canadian House of Commons to adopt for the same obvious reason that it was adopted in England, was not only adopted unanimously but not challenged by anybody. Do hon. members think if that change had been considered as an attempt to break with the best traditions of the House of Commons, as a danger to the working of parliamentary institutions, there would not have been found amongst those that I have named a single man to protest? But no, it passed unanimously.
The other portion of the rule, the one which exempts members from hearing the question, was challenged and, indeed, rather amusingly. The Conservative member who challenged the other part of the rule and said th-at the members should listen to the question, gave at the same time the evidence that that rule also had been disregarded for a good while in England, especially since the adoption of the new system of registering the vote by going through the lobbies. He said that time and again, he had heard members rushing into a lobby and asking friends of theirs; "What is all this about?"-"Biowed if I know!" Thus you had two informed members of the House of Commons pushing themselves into the lobby and coming out from the lobby into the House without knowing what they were voting for. For that reason it is better to discriminate, and here I give to the hon. member for Quebec East, the former Minister of Justice, (Mr. Lapointe), my reason for proposing this change. If we left it as it is, the whole of standing order 29 and the practice founded in England upon it, would apply to us. It would exempt members of the house from listening to a question. I do not believe in that, first for the reason that was given by Mr. Rutherford in England, but mainly because our mode of voting is not that which prevails in England. I claim, sir, that I am precisely within the spirit of British institutions when I say, as was stated time and time again by Sir John A. Macdonald and others, that all those rules and practices of the British parliament which are applicable to us we should endeavour to preserve, and those that are not applicable we should not. Therefore, I think that we should discard the first part of standing order 29 as adopted in England because not yet having resorted to the lobby system of voting it seems to me only
decent, were it only for the edification of the public, that a member should be in his seat when the question is put. I think that that is a conclusive reason why we should adopt that part of standing order 29 of the English house which concerns the liberty of members not to vote, but not the other part which allows them to vote without knowing upon what they are voting. Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), the motion standing in my name as it is recorded in the Votes and Proceedings.

speechtext:
I think, Mr. Speaker, that I voice the views of all the members of this house when I express our gratitude to the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) for the toil to which he has gone in bringing to the attention of the members the history of this rule. He has done it dispassionately, and I think with precision.
May I venture, however, to remind him that the reason why we in Canada are authorized to make such rules as we might desire for the government of our own house, provided that they did not exceed the power exercised in the making of rules by the House of Commons of Great Britain is to be found in the fact that when the British North America Act was originally passed it contained in section eighteen a clause which provided as follows:
The privileges, immunities, and powers to be held, enjoyed, and exercised by the Senate and by the House of Commons, and by the members therof respectively, shall be such as are from time to time defined by act of the parliament of Canada, but so that the same shall never exceed those at the passing of this act held, enjoyed, and exercised by the Commons House of 'Parliament of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, and by the members thereof.
That, in a very vital moment in our history, was found to stand in the way of the exercise of certain necessary powers, so in 1875, on the 19th of July, the imperial parliament amended the British North America Act by substituting a new section reading as follows:
The privileges, immunities, and powers to be held, enjoyed, and exercised by the Senate and by the House of Commons, and by the members thereof respectively, shall be such as are from time to time defined by act of the parliament of Canada, but so that any act of the parliament of Canada defining such privileges, immunities, and powers shall not confer any privileges, immunities, or powers exceeding those at the passing of such act held, enjoyed, and exercised by the Commons House of Parliament of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, and by the members thereof.
As the hon. member for Labelle has very properly pointed out, there was a rule in

Rules-Members Not Voting
England until recent years compelling members to vote. That rule was abrogated in 1906 under the circumstances to which the hon. gentleman has referred, and to which I shall presently make some reference. The original rule was based on the assumption that every member of the House of Commons should, if he were in his place, vote upon any given question that was submitted by the Speaker for the consideration of the house. Two factors influenced the commons in changing that rule, one was the confusion with respect to voting. The hon. gentleman has referred to that. As is well known, in England to vote a member leaves the chamber and goes into either the government or the opposition lobby. The tellers are appointed by the Speaker for the division. When several parties other than the two old parties, as the hon. gentleman has said, began to exercise authority there was first of all provision made, not by law, but by custom, for abstention from voting, and the reason that the rule was amended was because it was so wholly disregarded. That was the real reason. In other words, the confusion in voting and the difficulties in voting, by reason of there being but the (two lobbies, had brought about a situation that made it incumbent that the rules should be changed in the manner indicated.
In my opinion this is a matter which every member of ithe house should consider from the point of view of the best interests of the house. In my opinion every member of the house, if he is in the chamber, should record his view on every question submitted to the house by the Speaker. As I was thinking of this matter ithis morning I remembered the words of Burke:
I certainly have very warm wishes for the place of my birth, but the sphere of my duties is my true country.
Those of you who recall that celebrated 9peeeh of his to the electors of Bristol will recognize that he -put perhaps as fairly as it has ever been put the position of a member of parliament. The duty of a member of parliament is not only to his own constituency; it is to every part of this broad Dominion from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Once we have conceded the right of any member to withdraw from the chamber, then I think by the very nature of our proceedings and the method we adopt in voting, he must vote if he is in his place. I say that for two reasons:	First, because his	sitting	in	thischamber	when ithe question	is put	involvesmuch confusion if he does	not vote.	Youhave that here in this chamber yoursel-f, Mr. Speaker,	and it is known	to all	of	us.
Secondly, I conceive that there rests upon 
every member who thinks it worth while to sit in the chamber the duty to express to this country what his views are with respect to the questions so submitted to him. Does not that seem to be reasonable? In a vast country such as this where we have but 245 members, with questions which affect the well-being -of every part of the body politic constantly -being submitted for our consideration, and having by an extension of our rules given the right to a third group to move a subamendmen-t -when going into supply, thereby securing great freedom for -every individual in the expression of his opinion- is it not incumbent upon every one of us elected not only to represent a particular constituency, but to deal with problems that affeot the well-being of Canada as a whole, to express his opinion in the only method known to the law in which he can express it in this house, namely, by rising in his place and recording his opinion? While pairs are not recognized by parliamentary practice and procedure, the custom or convention has grown up whereby the view of a member paired is recorded upon the journals of the house. I cannot therefore do other than in a very few words indicate that I believe it is the bounden duty of every hon. member of the Canadian House of Commons, in view of the problems with which we have to deal, to be ready and willing if he sits in this house to express an opinion. If peradventure there be those who believe that it is undesirable for particular reasons at a given moment not to express an opinion, I see no reason why an hon. member might not withdraw from the house. I very distinctly recall an occasion in which I did. I felt that for the moment I was not in accord with the view held by my friends, and another hon. gentleman and myself retired from the chamber rather than vote. I was sitting in the seat now occupied by the former Minister of Marine (Mr. Cardin). In England it requires only seven or eight minutes to record a division, and in the English House of Commons there are about six hundred members. Those hon. members who have watched the clock realize how long it takes in this house. The provision for calling in the members in the Canadian House of Commons is somewhat different from the custom in England. In our house Mr. Speaker says, "Call in the members," and during the interval which elapses between the time the bell rings to call in the members and the Speaker rises to put the question there is a period given for hon. members to finally determine whether or not they will go into the lobby and not vote or be in the house and vote. I consider that interval to afford

Rules-Members Not Voting
opportunity to each hon. member to consider how he will vote-such an opportunity is not afforded in the same way in England. As Burke said in one of his addresses the English do not believe that customs which violate the law should long continue and the law is repealed. And so the custom by which the law was disregarded with respect to voting in England was crystallized by the repeal of the provisions which called upon members to vote.
We are a new country, with fresh problems, large obligations and responsibilities, and I do not believe there is in this house a single member who desires to escape his obligations or be relieved of his responsibilities. His obligations are ito Canada. His responsibilities are to the country as a whole and in the discharge of those obligations and responsibilities I believe it is in the best interests of this Dominion that every member of this house should, when the proper moment comes, rise in his place and express his opinion upon every question submitted from the chair. If he does not wish to do that he should withdraw from the chamber and thereby preserve his independence of mind and freedom of choice hereafter. That is my conviction in the matter.
Holding these views as strongly as I do I now move an amendment to the motion made by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) seconded by Mr. Stevens as follows:
That the motion be amended by striking out the word "not" therein before the word "obi iged."

so that hereafter, whatever doubt may have been entertained in the past, it will be removed and all hon. members in this house will be obliged to vote when the question is put from the chair.

speechtext: There is no doubt that my hon. friend from Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) is correct in his interpretation of the situation as it exists. So much is clear. From the words of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister there is no doubt a mistake has been made, and now it is proposed to correct that mistake by enacting a new rule. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I had no intention of taking part in this discussion had it not been for the remarks of the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil), who is a very old and experienced member of this house, who for a period of years was the first commoner, and for whose judgments and opinions I have a very high respect. Writh the principle involved in the amendment moved by the Prime Minister, I am in hearty accord. And I feel that all thinking members, if they dissociate themselves from certain events which occurred in this house last week, on calm reflection will agree that every man sent to the House of Commons, representing as he does not only his constituents, but the people of Canada as a whole, should have an opinion and be prepared to stand behind his opinion by his vote on every vital question that comes before the house. For that reason I intend to vote for the amendment, but I hope the Prime Minister will pause for a moment and give heed to the suggestion-it was merely a suggestion as I understand it-made by the hon. member for Bonaventure. We have a system of pairs that has been in force for many years. This system is a great convenience to all gentlemen in this house. I for one feel that I could not carry on my parliamentary duties unless I had a permanent pair for each and every session. Members who have interests outside the house are often called away at a moment's notice to fulfil other duties of an imperative nature. I suggest to the Prime Minister that he give consideration to the proposal made by my hon. friend from Bonaventure, so that a member who has a registered pair may still sit in his place and not vote, and yet have his name appear in Hansard as having been present. I understand from my reading that in England a member of parliament is judged very largely by his constituents, not by the number of speeches he makes in the House of Commons, but by the number of times he is present and records his vote. I commend this to some of those gentlemen who talk so much in this house; let them remember that actions speak louder than words. I again suggest to the Prime Minister that he give heed to the proposal of the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) in order that some way may be found whereby those members who are paired and are present will not have to walk out of the house.

Yes. We have had occasion to study the rule and we have studied it; and we knew perfectly well that the rule became obsolete in Great Britain in 1906. We knew that we were following the British practice in respect of that rule, and we knew also that we had the ruling of a previous Speaker on the matter. So that I knew when I made that declaration that I was observing the rules of the house and was the only man who was keeping them. The hon. gentlemen whom the Sergeant at Arms should have tapped on the shoulder were the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the two whips; for the Speaker had given his ruling before they spoke and they disregarded it, trying to press upon us an old and obsolete rule which had been discarded in England and ruled against by a Speaker of this house. I am glad, therefore, of the opportunity of making my position clear, and I trust that members of the press gallery, who knew as little about the rides as some hon. members of the house did, will take note of this and see that we are apologized to in the press.
With regard to the amendment, it is now seeking the authority which this house lacked on Tuesday night. That is the meaning of the amendment, and I take it, therefore, as an excellent apology to this corner. And as regards pairs, I hope that this rule, if it passes, will abolish the practice of having pairs. In that event, hon. gentlemen will be in a worse position than we are when we are compelled to walk out of the chamber.

maintopic: RULES OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT DECLARING RIGHT OP MEMBERS TO REFRAIN FROM VOTING
speechtext:
It seems to me that the house is attaching more importance to this question than it deserves, because whether the main motion or the amendment carries, the result is practically the same. If I believed with my right hon. friend the Prime Minister that the institutions of British government and parliamentary practice were in serious danger unless the amendment carried, I should be disposed to vote with him. But surely that [DOT]cannot be the case when, as is well known, and as has been stated here, in the British parliament members are not compelled to vote. And no one claims that parliamentary or representative institutions are endangered thereby.
But I have three chief reasons for being opposed to the amendment proposed by the Prime Minister. In the first place, I do not

believe very much in compulsion except where it is necessary in the public interest. Secondly, I conceive that it is quite possible that a member may conscientiously refrain from voting, not having so crystallized his opinion on a question as to warrant his voting one way or the other. And in the third place -and this is as important as the other two reasons, if not more so-if the amendment carries and hon. members are compelled to vote in the event of their remaining in the chamber, it is quite easy for them to evade the question after all by simply absenting themselves from the chamber. After all, why should it be necessary for a member to leave the chamber in order to avoid being compelled to vote?
Mr. LaVER'GNE : May I ask the hon. member a question for information? Suppose a member does not leave the chamber: If his vote is not recorded, how are we to know the difference between those who are absent from the chamber and those who have not voted, being present, because they lacked courage or conviction?

maintopic: RULES OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT DECLARING RIGHT OP MEMBERS TO REFRAIN FROM VOTING
speechtext:
The argument has been advanced that a man should be compelled to vote if he stays in the chamber. But if he leaves the chamber you do not know what his views are on the question. Let me say that his constituents will know what position he takes on certain questions; and the mere fact that he is in the chamber and declines to vote makes his attitude more conspicuous than possibly it would be if he left the chamber.
Mr. LaVERGNE: But under the rules his views would not be recorded.

maintopic: RULES OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT DECLARING RIGHT OP MEMBERS TO REFRAIN FROM VOTING
speechtext:
My hon. friend knows very
well that, with the press gallery in full operation, and with his friends listening to and observing him, his constituents through the press will soon know that such a member declined to vote. My right hon. friend has also stated that he is in favour of the amendment for the reason that, if members remain in the chamber and do not vote, it leads to confusion. I cannot see the point of that argument. If there is any confusion whatever it must be because of some difficulty in the taking of the vote by the assistant clerk. But any difficulty that he might have in that regard is certainly also present in the case of those who abstain from voting because they are paired. We do not recognize pairs, and I cannot see that there could be any possible confusion, so far as taking the vote is concerned, if certain members were absolved altogether from voting.

I have given the reasons for
my attitude. I am opposed in principle to the idea of compelling members to vote; I think they should be free. My mind is open, however. I do not think that the matter need necessarily be decided here, nor do I see any reason why we should not adopt the practice that has been frequently followed m similar cases. I am going to propose a subamendment, and if it does not carry I shall certainly have to oppose the amendment moved by the Prime Minister. My proposal is that the matter be referred to a committee for report to the house. If that proposal is not adopted, I shall have to vote against the amendment and in support of the motion made by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa). My motion is:
That all the words after "that" in the amendment be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"all the words after 'that' in the main motion be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
a committee of the house be appointed to act with Mr. Speaker for the purpose of considering the question of amending the standing orders of the house by adding the following:
'9a. Upon a division, a member is not nbliged to vote.' "

maintopic: RULES OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT DECLARING RIGHT OP MEMBERS TO REFRAIN FROM VOTING
speechtext:
I will vote against the subamendment. The issue is a clear one, and if the house cannot settle a simple question like that we had better go home. Although I was seconder of the motion proposed by my deskmate (Mr. Bourassa) I did not intend to speak upon it until there was an amendment, for the reason that my hon. friend covered the ground so thoroughly and clearly that it was not possible to say anything without repeating his arguments. But since the amendment has been moved, I should like to say a few words. The amendment compels members to vote, and the Prime Minister put forward some arguments in support of that proposal. He drew a comparison with the British House of Commons, where they vote by going into lobbies; and if I followed him rightly he said that when more than two parties arose it led to confusion because the
members of the third or fourth party objected to going into one or other of the lobbies. The same condition exists here. While we do not go into a lobby, we are asked to vote yes or no, which is exactly the same proposition. I do not see any strength in that argument. Then again he told us that of late years the rules had been changed in this house and it was now possible to move an amendment and subamendment to going into supply, and upon one or two other occasions, and that, he said, afforded a full opportunity for the expression of views by the groups opposite.
I would point out to the house that there are now at least five groups on this side and the possibility of their being allowed to move one subamendment does not give them an opportunity of expressing their views. They may be peculiar views, but nevertheless they are the views of the group and there is just as much reason to allow five groups to express their views as there is to allow two or three.
On the question of pairs the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) read out of the records of the house where Sir John A. Macdonald, in dealing with this very point, said that in spite of pairs hon. members would be compelled to vote. Sir John said that the rules read that wherever an hon. member had got into the house inadvertently he would be compelled to break faith with the man with whom he was paired. Here is the situation which now exists. An hon. member on this side pairs with an hon. member opposite; he is obliging the hon. member, and when it comes to a vote, under present conditions, he stays in his place. He does not vote, but after the vote has been taken he rises in his place and says:	I was paired with the hon.
member for so-and-so, if I had voted I would have voted in such a way, and that remark is recorded in Hansard. That serves a double purpose, it reveals to his constituents the fact that he was in the house and paying attention to his duties on that occasion, and reveals what his intention in the matter was. That safeguards him and allows him to be courteous to his opponent.
If this rule is introduced the member who is paired will have to absent himself and there will be no record that he was even in Ottawa on the day of the vote. I have known worse things to happen in the heat of party politics than for someone to get up and say: "Why the hon. gentleman was not even in the house when the vote was taken", quite regardless of the fact that that apparent absence was only an act of courtesy to an hon.

Rules-Members Not Voting
member opposite. It would lead to the doing away with pairs and to confusion and injustice in connection therewith.
I have always voted when I was in the house, and so far as I know, I intend always to do so. I recall the remarks of some great man, I forget now who he was, who said to his opponent:	"I bitterly oppose your sentiments but I will fight to the death for the right for you to utter them". That is the view I take in this matter. Whether or not I approve of abstaining from voting, I am prepared to fight to any reasonable extent in support of the views of those who wish either to vote or to abstain from voting. As the hon. member for Labelle said the other evening, the privileges of one are the privileges of all.
There is too great a disposition in this house, and there always has been ever since I have been in it, to curtail the privileges and rights of the individual private member. To-day it is almost impossible for a private member to introduce a bill and get it carried through to completion; it is possible by the very simplest intrigue to prevent its passage. Another good illustration occurred a few years ago when we agreed to cut down the time of speaking to forty minutes. During the debate on the address I have been grimly amused in observing that almost every hon. member who got up and deplored the fact that he had only forty minutes in which to speak, voted on that occasion for the passage of that rule, while I and a few other hon. members opposed it.
Why not let us follow the practice followed in Great Britain? The Prime Minister says that the other practice had been followed for three hundred years before they changed it and that we are a young country. Because we are a young country there is no reason why we should move three hundred years behind Great Britain. Why not take advantage of Great Britain's experience which has led her to change her rules after trying them out for three hundred years? Is that not a very good argument in support of the assertion that there was wisdom in their action and that we should be well advised to take a similar step? Why should not we follow in her footsteps?
Therefore, while I have no wish or intention to abstain from voting in the house, I will vote in support of those who wish so to abstain.
Mr. ARMAND LaVERGNE (Montmagny): Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great attention to the hon. member who has just spoken CM. Neill), but although we have been
]Mr. Neill.]
waiting for an expression from the other side as to the reason why an hon. member present in the house should abstain from voting, I must say that I have not heard that reason expressed. We are allowed a motion, an amendment and very often a subamendment and I should think there would be opportunity afforded to hon. members whose conscience may be rather delicate to make a fair choice. I understand there may be cases where an hon. member cannot find a choice suits him either in the motion, the amendment or the subamendment, and that is why I put the question: Why should an hon. member who stays in the house abstain from voting? Another hon. member may be absent from force of circumstances, and should this motion carry the votes and proceedings would place the hon. member who abstained from voting either because his conscience had not been enlightened sufficiently or from lack of conviction or courage, upon the same footing as the hon. member who had been forced to absent himself. Unless we change our whole proces verbal, the hon. member who is in the house and who abstains from voting because he has found no motion to his choice will be absolutely in the same position as the hon. member who is forced to be absent but who would have had the courage to vote had he not been prevented from attending in the chamber. I have tried to find a reason for supporting the motion of the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), but I have been unable to do so. When an hon. member is present in the house and does not desire to vote, there is only one thing to do; instead of sitting in his place, he should step out.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: RULES OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT DECLARING RIGHT OP MEMBERS TO REFRAIN FROM VOTING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having in mind what he had to say, I am rather surprised that the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) found it necessary to introduce any motion. He made his position quite clear, and I believe he convinced the house that he is in the right in the position he takes with respect to the present rule being as he describes it. He has, however, introduced a motion, an amendment has been proposed to it, and an amendment to the amendment has also been proposed. We are now in the position that with respect to these several motions we have either to rise and make clear where we stand, or refrain from voting by abstaining, as apparently that is now permissible, in which latter event no one in the country will know just where we stand on this all important question. Inasmuch as I believe in members of the house indicating to the country where they stand on all questions that come before the house, I do not propose to avoid voting on any of these motions, but I wish to state where I stand in regard to the subamendment which is before the house and, if need be, later on with respect to the amendment and the main motion.
I would ask whether this is not the right moment to consider following to the full, the British practice and custom. As nearly as I can make out from the discussion which we have had this afternoon, such embarrassment as has arisen in different quarters of the house has arisen from the fact that in one particular we follow the British practice and in another we do not. The British practice is to record the votes by members leaving the chamber and passing to the right or to the left of the Speaker. Their votes are recorded by tellers. Only those votes are recorded which refer to the names of hon. members who have passed the chair. If any hon. member does not wish to vote, he may remain in the house. That is what my hon. friends in the far corner
wish to do, I understand, on many questions; they wish to stay in the house and refrain from voting. I would suggest that the amendment to the amendment which has been moved by the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler), proposing the reference of the whole matter to a committee of the house, be supported by the house, having in view a consideration at this time as to whether we should not adopt the British practice with respect to the recording of votes. I believe if that step were taken, it would solve the difficulties of practically all parties or groups in the house. Those who believe in members indicating to the country where they stand, will, if the British practice is followed, have their position known by passing to the right or to the left of the Speaker. Those who wish to refrain from voting, and at the same time remain in the house, will be able to abstain and to remain.
There is one other reason why I suggest that that course should be followed now and it is in reference to the subject of pairs which has been raised by the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) and spoken to by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson). The directing of the attention of His Honour the Speaker to hon. members who have not voted has to be taken before the announcement of the vote is made. Obviously it is impossible for one, looking on, to read in the mind of an hon. member whether he has abstained from voting because he is paired or because he does not wish to vote. If hereafter an effort is to be made to find out which of the two reasons has actuated hon. members who may have refrained from voting, there will be endless confusion. If the practice is followed whereby members pass to the right or to the left of the Speaker, then, with respect to pairs, all that would be necessary that pairs might be recorded would be for the whips to hand a list of the pairs to the tellers and have them subsequently recorded in the proceedings. That would indicate how every member who was paired had intended to vote. It would meet what the hon. member for York-Sunbury has in mind, of making sure that pairs are recorded while at the same time preserving to hon. members an honourable obligation between them to abstain, in certain circumstances, from voting.
A further point I would make is this: the time that is taken up in the house in calling and recording names is considerable. There is a great waste of time in recording votes by calling individual names and causing members to rise in their places, while the names are being recorded and then subsequently

Rules-Members Rot Voting
counting up the totals. I believe we would save the time of the house-and surely we need to save all the time we can-by adopting this speedier method of simply walking into the lobbies, having the vote thus recorded, and allowing the journals of the house to indicate what action the different members have taken. It is for that reason that I would strongly urge hon. members to support the amendment to the amendment. If the amendment to the amendment went the length of a general revision of the rules of the house, I would object to it. I do not think it is necessary at this time to open up the rules generally, but the concrete motion that is before the house might well be referred to a committee in language sufficiently broad to permit of its consideration in relation to the larger proposal.
Before taking my seat, may I say that I resent very strongly the imputation of the leader of the group in the far corner, the so-called Independent group, that amendments moved by one or other of the old parties in the house are moved for reasons of party politics, pure and simple. I will remind my hon. friend that long before there were any third parties or independent groups in the house, the custom in parliament was for members of a political party to express their views in the form of motions and amendments to motions. This was and is the one and only method where a vote is to be recorded. It ill becomes my hon. friend to impute a motive of that kind to any hon. member or to any political party. May I just say to him, and to those who take that view, that the fact that they do impute such a motive to others makes me feel very strongly that something of the kind is in their own minds? If there ever was a playing of party politics with respect to public questions, it will be found in relation to more than one of the subamendments which have been moved by the so-called independent groups in the house.

maintopic: RULES OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT DECLARING RIGHT OP MEMBERS TO REFRAIN FROM VOTING
speechtext:
This question affects not only the rights of members of parliament, which are not greatly jeopardized, but the rights of the electors of the country. The people have a right to know the views of every member of parliament on every question that comes before the house. All these subterfuges are simply methods to enable the members of the house to shirk their duties. Look at the array of talent in the press gallery. What are they there for? They are there to enlighten the people of Canada as to the views of the respective members on every question that comes before the house. I for one do not wish 
to shirk that responsibility. It is up to every hon. member to record his vote on every question that comes before us.
I am very much in sympathy with the amendment moved by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), with the exception that some provision should -be made for pairs. But I think sometimes we forget the great past, the grave responsibilities that have come down to this house. When we study the history of parliamentary government, what does it mean? If we go back hundreds of years, what did they fight for? First it was for parliamentary government; second, for the supremacy of the House of Commons, and, third, that the House of Commons should represent the people. How are the people who send us here to know whether we represent the people of this great Dominion or not if provision is made for every hon. member to shirk the recording of his opinion upon any question that comes before the house? There are at least three ways now open to a member: one is to record his vote; a second is to pair with another member, and the third is to absent himself from the house. Every member knows that to-day a man who shirks his vote in the house has to bear the disgrace of that before his electors. They look upon it as an act of cowardice. This is only opening another door whereby a member may shirk his duty. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the amendment of the Prime Minister should carry, so that every member of the house who is present when a vote is taken shall have to stand up and record his vote.

I had no
intention of taking part in this debate, but the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. McGibbon) has made a statement which should not pass unchallenged. I should like to remind him that his own leader a short time ago said very frankly that last year he deliberately walked out of the chamber to avoid taking part in a vote. If there was a little more thinking behind some of the talking that is done in this house-

-we should not have so much confusion, and that applies to some of the things that were said by hon. members opposite last Tuesday night.
The Prime Minister in moving his amendment made some reference to the confusion that is caused in the house by members not voting. I would like to point out that last Tuesday night, when this confusion is said

Rules-Members Not Voting
to have taken place, you were called upon, Mr. Speaker, at one time to get up and remonstrate with some members of the house because of their disorderly conduct. speechtext:
There is one other matter
to which I wish to refer. I was under the impression, as were other hon. members, that a year ago both the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition were rather in favour of changing the method of taking the vote in this house, so I think the Prime Minister would be very well advised to accept the subamendment and allow this matter to go to a committee to see if we cannot get a better method of taking the vote. It may be that the committee would recommend the method used in the British house. I do not know whether that method is the best or not, but I certainly think that all sides of the house are agreed that we need a new method, and I would suggest to the Prime Minister that he take that into consideration before he makes up his mind to press his own amendment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: RULES OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT DECLARING RIGHT OP MEMBERS TO REFRAIN FROM VOTING
speechtext:
The subamendment is
predicated, I submit, upon an entirely erroneous impression of the situation. The right hon. leader of the opposition has suggested that he was left in some doubt as to why the hon. member for Labelle moved his motion. I confess that I have had doubts as to the wisdom of it because it has precipitated this question into the house, and it must now be decided. The question to be decided is: Shall members vote or not, when they are in the house?
There is a singular misunderstanding on the part of a great many members as to what the obligation of a member is. I wonder how many have read standing order 5. It reads:
Every member is bound to attend the service of the house, unless leave of absence has been given him by the house.
That is the rule.

maintopic: RULES OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT DECLARING RIGHT OP MEMBERS TO REFRAIN FROM VOTING
speechtext: What about the Prime Minister?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: RULES OF THE HOUSE

speechtext:
Exactly; he is bound to
be in his place at the opening of the house.

maintopic: RULES OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT DECLARING RIGHT OP MEMBERS TO REFRAIN FROM VOTING
speechtext:
It does not say the
opening.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: RULES OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT DECLARING RIGHT OP MEMBERS TO REFRAIN FROM VOTING
speechtext:
Wait till I give you the rest of it. Paragraph 53 of Beauchesne's Rules and Forms comments on that standing order as follows:
A member _ of the British house was expelled, in 1715, for refusing to attend the service of the house.
Paragraph 54 says:
In case of unavoidable absence it was for several years usual, in the Canadian House of Commons, to have the reasons explained to the house and leave then given to the member to absent himself from his duties.
There is the standing order, and I fancy that is the reason why most of us try to be here at prayers.
Having had this question precipitated into the house, may I make this further observation with respect to what was said by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner). My statement the other evening and that of the leader of the opposition was based upon the defiance of the rules of the house by certain members of the house. It was not a statement as to the wisdom of the rule. The Speaker having decided as he did, it was perfectly obvious that for any member to defy his ruling was not the proper method under our institutions of dealing with the matter. If hon. members had desired to appeal from his ruling, an appeal could have been taken. But certainly it could not be done by defiance. I did say what I believed then and still believe, that nothing is better calculated to drag the whole institution of parliament into disrepute than to have members speak of it in just that way. That was my objection, and that of others who followed me, and I am sure that it is the reason why the hon. member for Labelle referred to this whole matter in the way he did. He said that that was but an incident; but what is larger than the incident is the principle involved.
The subamendment does not afford an opportunity to discuss the method of voting. Let the hon. member for Macleod have no misunderstanding as to that. By the subamendment a committee is asked to deal with a very simple question. For once I am wholly in accord with the hon. member for Comox-

Rules-Members Not Voting
Alberni (Mr. Neill) when he said, "I feel capable of dealing with this matter without asking a committee to deal with it for me." The whole question is this: Shall we be obliged to vote or not? I have given at some length the reasons that induced me to believe that we should. If the members of the house think that we should not, it will be found I think that to refer this to a committee is merely to invite a few gentlemen to meet together and discuss among themselves how you or I should determine for himself a question that is personal to himself.

maintopic: RULES OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT DECLARING RIGHT OP MEMBERS TO REFRAIN FROM VOTING
speechtext: Would it be competent so to enlarge the subamendment as to make it possible for the committee to canvass other methods of taking the vote?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: RULES OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT DECLARING RIGHT OP MEMBERS TO REFRAIN FROM VOTING
speechtext: It certainly would be competent to enlarge the subamendment so as to involve many things that it does not now involve. At least half a dozen members of this house have studied the different methods of voting. I recall a conversation that I had with the right hon. leader of the opposition after having watched the British House of Commons divide. I am free to say that I took considerable time one afternoon when we were waiting on a committee at Westminster to ascertain just how the voting did take place in the British House of Commons. The vote is over in seven or eight minutes, as we all know. Our lobbies seem to me to be reasonably well adapted to that purpose. But there is nothing that a committee can do with respect to it. It is well known how the voting is done in the British house. The Speaker names the tellers, the ayes go to the right and the nays to the left, and the tellers report back. I saw the changes which have been made in recent years because of difficulties in counting. The whole matter was carried on simply and effectively. I did think that we might try it here as an experiment, but I am not convinced that it would be a successful experiment at the moment. I am bound to say that I do not think that anything a committee can do can be more than has already been stated in this house so many times. If it is the opinion of the house that the method of taking the vote should be changed, I for one should be very glad to afford the opportunity for members to decide whether or not the present method should be abolished and a different method should be used, but for the moment the question is: Shall a member who is in the chamber vote or not, and upon that issue I propose, as far as it goes, to vote.

maintopic: RULES OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT DECLARING RIGHT OP MEMBERS TO REFRAIN FROM VOTING
speechtext: May I remark that in my experience during the twenty-seven years I have been in the house the rules have never been changed or altered except-

maintopic: RULES OF THE HOUSE

maintopic: RULES OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT DECLARING RIGHT OP MEMBERS TO REFRAIN FROM VOTING
speechtext: Yes, through a committee especially appointed for that purpose, with the one exception of the occasion when closure was introduced. As my hon. friend knows there was an emergency at the time to require that special procedure. Why not in this instance proceed as we have always done and follow the practice which has always been followed by the house? Surely there is no emergency in the present instance. We might very well observe the tradition that the rules of the house should not be changed except after consideration by a committee. My learned and hon. friend must realize that in the present instance there is nothing at issue with the exception of one particular question. If it were other than that, if it were a question of setting out a new rule, the circumstances would be different. Since, however, the question has been raised in the house by an hon. member, we are bound to deal with it.

maintopic: RULES OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT DECLARING RIGHT OP MEMBERS TO REFRAIN FROM VOTING
speechtext:
The answer of the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) at least gives me an excuse for speaking to this matter. I am inclined to agree with him that the subamendment of the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) is rather too restrictive in its nature. As it is worded the proposed committee can decide only yes or no on the main motion of the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa). However the amendment of my right hon. friend the leader of the house would seem to exclude ithe practice of pairing. The amendment .to my mind is quite fair in that it says that every hon. member in the house must vote. This is a new regulation being introduced into the rules which govern the conduct of this house. It will be in vain that we refer to the age old custom of pairing which has been followed. Mr. Speaker will say to us, and I think quite properly, that we

Rules-Members Not Voting
have passed a new rule which precludes us from taking advantage of that custom. There is the broad question as to whether or not hon. members in the house shall vote. On that particular point I am in substantial and hearty agreement with the Prime Minister. It seems to me however if there is one occasion when a member might freely absent himself from the house and not vote it is when he is faced with three alternative proposals such as those we have before us today. Not one of them satisfies me, and I think many hon. members are in a similar position. May I suggest that if the Prime Minister would for a few minutes discuss the matter with the hon. member for North Waterloo it might be possible to evolve a subamendment which would refer to a committee on rules the question of the method of voting.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext:
The Prime Minister says
"no". Very well, but I think there should be consideration of the matter of drafting an amendment to our rule which would meet the views of the Prime Minister and those of the vast majority of hon. members in the house who wish every member to vote but who wish also to retain the privilege of pairing which we have enjoyed in the past.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: RULES OF THE HOUSE

speechtext: With the consent of the house I should like to add one word further. I suggest that the house permit one of the hon. gentlemen to my right to move the adjournment of this debate, and instead of having a committee we could talk this matter over and see if some provision of a satisfactory nature cannot be made.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: RULES OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT DECLARING RIGHT OP MEMBERS TO REFRAIN FROM VOTING
speechtext: I move the adjournment of the debate.

maintopic: RULES OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT DECLARING RIGHT OP MEMBERS TO REFRAIN FROM VOTING
speechtext:
Before the debate is adjourned I desire to say a few words, in the spirit in which I introduced the motion. First I thank the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) for the absolute vindication he has given of my attitude. There cannot be any better evidence that hon. members in this comer of the house were observing the rules as they have been interpreted by yourself and your predecessors, sir, than the amendment of the Prime Minister to-day providing that, in the future, we must not do what the other day was pointed to as constituting a violation of the rules. The action of the Prime Minister answers the objection of my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and that of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) that I was wrong in introducing my motion. If the rules of the house were and are as outlined in my proposal, then it follows that hon. members in this comer of the house were right the other day when they refused to vote, and that Mr. Speaker was right when he sustained them in their attitude. However, I shall not insist upon that.
There are one or two points to which I wish to refer before the debate is closed, because evidently it will be closed for this year. I introduced the motion in the first place because it was the only way of rectifying the wrong impression which has been created by the press of nearly all parties all over the country that a certain number of hon. members in this house, with whom I was counted, gave an awful example of rebellion against the rules of the house and the decision of Mr. Speaker. By choosing the only means at my disposal to have the house settle the question the press may now be informed, and I hope will inform the public, that those hon. gentlemen and the hon. lady who refused the other day to vote acted strictly in accordance with the rules of the house and the jurisprudence established by two speakers of the House of Commons. After all, the honour of all members in this house is dear to them, and it is their right to have such honour vindicated. I think every member, whatever his party differences may be, has no desire to have any of his fellow members, regardless of party, bandied all over the country as unruly persons and fit to be expelled from the house. And why? Because, forsooth, they observed the rules of the house.
Next I should like to refer to the question of paim. In the event of the amendment moved by the leader of the government carrying there could be no doubt left that any hon. member sitting in this house would either have to vote, regardless of the fact that he was paired, or step out of the house. How are we going to lay down the rule which the leader of the government says-mind you, I am not entirely opposed to his views-would oblige every hon. member sitting in the house to vote? Are we to impose that rule upon men who, rightly or wrongly, but in the fulness of their conviction and their conscience, believe that they cannot or must not vote? Are we going to apply the rule to them and not apply it to hon. members who, for their own personal convenience or to suit their business interests or professional callings, make arrangement through the whips to exempt themselves from
Buies-Members Not Voting

that duty which, according to the Prime Minister, is the bounden duty of every member of parliament? If the rule applies to members of parliament who do not seek refuge behind the practice of pairing in order to attend to their private affairs in preference to their public duties, then is the rule to remain inapplicable in cases of pairs?
Various hon. members whose names I will not give, because I wish to keep this debate on a friendly basis, have insinuated that hon. members who remained in the house and did not vote lacked courage. It may be that at times such action would amount to lack of courage. Also it may be a lack of courage when some hon. members vote against their personal convictions, because their party has voted that way. We are all subject to such weaknesses. Let no party or no hon. member of any party in this house pose as a Pharisee, We are all human and subject to mistakes. I confess I am subject to them in a retail and wholesale way. I beg however of the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition not to pose as the sole caretakers of the virtues of parliament; they also make their mistakes. My friends to the left, from my point of view, make their mistakes. From the point of view of all, I make mistakes, I admit. But I repeat, whether we belong to one party or the other, we are all here because we have been elected by the people of Canada to vote or not to vote according to our conscience and our convictions.
The Prime Minister has repeated the well-known argument that the right of any member to move a subamendment offers him ample freedom. I say no. I repeat, and I insist upon it, that once the subamendment has been disposed of, you must vote for or against what is before you, the unamended motion or amendment. If that contains things of which you approve and things of which you disapprove, I. ask again:	How then can
jmu justify the iron rule which you desire to impose upon the inherent right of a member of parliament, to vote for something of which he disapproves, if the motion necessarily contains something against his conscience or his convictions? With regard to the right of the electors to see *whether we vote or not, that is a matter to be arranged between each member of parliament and his electors when he appeals to the final judgment of the people. But so long as we remain in this house, until the next time the people pass judgment upon the government, upon the opposition, upon the second opposition and upon the free-for-

alls or the independent members, so long as we are here, I claim there should be one rule or none. So far as I am concerned, I prefer the rule proposed by the Prime Minister to no rule at all. If it is to be the rule, very well, I am prepared to accept it. I will vote against it; but suppose it is adopted, I think it better to have it rather than to be in the absurd position in -which we found ourselves when members were threatened with expulsion from the house because they chose to exercise a right which on all sides is now acknowledged to be incontestable. I claim that this should not happen again, therefore I would rather have the amendment moved by the Prime Minister than no rule at all. But may I respectfully tell the right hon. Prime Minister that in moving that amendment he is resorting to another part of himself which is not the result of his study of British law, or of British practice, which is not the result of his British spirit; but that in this as in some other instances he is letting himself follow his autocratic instinct and his stand for an iron rule instead of the broad interpretation which has been followed for over thirty years in the British house and which has been followed in this house from 1927 until 1931.
Just one further word. The Prime Minister has quoted rule 5, which makes it an obligation on all members to attend to all sittings of the house. That is quite true. It is an old rule and was in effect all along previous to 1867. Any student of the old records could find therein that at any session of parliament no member could absent himself without having the leave of the house, and that leave was recorded in the journals. Are the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition prepared every day to draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the absence of their various followers, whether they are paired or not? That rule does not acknowledge pairs. If that rule applies, no member has the right to go to Montreal or to Toronto to plead a case; nor, although paired with the member for Muskoka-Ontario or for some other constituency, can a member stay in his seat mum and for the time being suspend his functions as a member in order to enable another gentleman to go to Montreal or to Toronto to attend to his private business. If that is to be the rule, then let it be applied to all; let it be applied to pleading lawyers, let it be applied to bankers, let it be applied to merchants, let it be applied to members for near constituencies while our colleagues from the

Unemployment Situation
far distant western and eastern provinces have to stay here, Sundays included. That is my sole answer, and I think it ought to be sufficient.
I thank the house, Mr. Speaker, for the manner in which it has received my humble suggestion. I do not think the time spent on this debate has been lost, because it has shown the necessity of clarifying a situation which in the future, as last week, could have given birth to disagreeable incidents. As far as that is concerned, I thank again the leader of the government and the leader of the opposition for their timely suggestion. I hope it will materialize sooner than other pious intentions that have been expressed many times to have a complete revision of the manner in which votes are recorded in this house; and also dealing with the question of pairs, not from the viewpoint of individual convenience, but from the viewpoint of public trust and interest, which has been so eloquently pointed out this afternoon by the leader of the house.
