Mr. Speaker,
I should like to ask the acting Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) which of two reports that appear in the press to-day from the Canadian Press is correct, if either. One is dated Hamilton, Ontario, April 27. The other, Montreal, of the same date. I am quoting from the report as it appears in the Ottawa Citizen:
Sees Unemployment Problem Diminishing Senator Gideon Robertson Speaks at Hamilton
Hamilton, Ont., April 27.-"In Canada the unemployment problem is diminishing," declared Senator Gideon Robertson, federal minister of labour, addressing the Hamilton Chamber of Commerce at its annual meeting here to-night.
"We have experienced the most distressing winter in many years, but we emerge into the sunlight of hope at the beginning of another season, and it is within the realm of reason to say that, before the snow falls again, our worries will have largely disappeared," he declared.
In the same paper there is a despatch from Montreal:
Thinks Relief Plan To Be Repeated By Government Next Winter
Montreal, April 27.-A conversation he had with Senator Gideon Robertson, Dominion Minister of Labour, led him to believe the Dominion authorities would repeat for next winter their unemployment relief, Alderman W. H. Biggar, leader of the Montreal city council, stated to-day.
By this he meant that the Dominion government would again vote twenty million dollars for relief work, the provinces paying twenty millions and municipalities 40 millions.
I wish my hon. friend would advise the house as to which of these reports, if either, is correct.

that it is expedient to amend the Customs Act in respect to discounts or deductions to be allowed in estimating the value for duty; to provide for power to examine witnesses on oath, and to pay their reasonable travelling expenses; and for the imposition of penalties and prevention of smuggling operations.
He said: The bill which will be introduced upon the passage of this resolution deals with departmental amendments for the purpose of carrying out efficiently the terms of the present Customs Act. The resolution in its first two lines would seem to signify some serious amendment in respect of deductions to be allowed in estimating the value of duty, but in fact it simply deals with a difficulty which has arisen in the preparation of invoices submitted by importers which have been prepared by merchants and salesmen in foreign countries. The section of the act which is to be amended is section 3 of chapter 2 of the statutes of 1930, second session. That section will be amended by the insertion of
the words "and deducted" in a certain part of the section, which will make it more clear and facilitate the administration of the act. The amendment does not deal with any principle or policy, but with a difficulty which has arisen in its administration by the department.
The other amendments suggested are almost exclusively amendments which were previously suggested during the regime of the former Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler). The hon. gentleman had a bill drawn up by the department dealing with certain difficulties which had arisen, but owing to the time which elapsed before the prorogation of parliament, I am informed by the departmental officers that no opportunity was afforded for its introduction. The present minister has adopted it almost word for word, with the addition of one or two suggestions. One suggestion is that certain affidavits may now be taken by trade commissioners abroad as well as by other persons authorized to administer oaths in affidavits for use in this country.
Another amendment which my hon. friend had prepared provides that the assistant commissioner of customs may exercise certain powers of the minister as well as of the commissioner of customs. Owing to a vast increase in the business of the department during recent years, of which no one is better informed than is my hon. friend, it has been deemed wise that in certain matters the assistant commissioner of customs may act when the commissioner of customs is otherwise engaged.
Another suggestion deals with inquiries to be held by officers of the department. That suggestion is new to this parliament, but I understand it was previously made by the hon. gentleman in connection with the draft bill of 1930.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS AMENDMENT TO MOTION OP MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
it is my intention before you leave the chair to bring to the notice of the house a question that we deem to be of prime importance, namely the position of agriculture in this country. I may say that before I sit down I shall move an amendment to the motion to go into supply.

Agricultural Conditions
If any apology were necessary for bringing this question to the attention of the house at this time, it would be found in the speech made a few days ago by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett). But no such apology is necessary; indeed that speech, in which he sought to give to the people of Canada the impression that there were no serious conditions existing in relation to agriculture, has made it incumbent upon us to bring this matter to the attention of the house. Members who are in touch with agricultural conditions not only on the prairies but throughout Canada, members who really know what the position of the farmer is, heard with amazement the statement made by the Prime Minister, and I can well believe that that speech caused not only amazement but consternation among his supporters in the house and outside of it. If I correctly estimate the way in which that speech has been received by the people of the country, I can say that they view it, not only with amazement and consternation, but with the utmost indignation. It is true that we heard similar statements made by the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Turnbull), the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. MacMillan), the hon. member for Long Lake (Mr. Cowan), and hon. members from other parts of the west, but we did not attach a great deal of importance to the statements made by those hon. gentlemen. When, however, the Prime Minister of Canada, from his place in the house, makes an effort to show that there are no serious conditions confronting agriculture; that agriculture is not in a precarious state, and when he undertakes to show that whatever may be wrong is entirely the fault of the farmer himself for having indulged too freely in speculation, then it is time for us to take notice.
But when we see the evidence upon which the Prime Minister bases his conclusions, we see how hopelessly he has failed to appreciate the true condition of agriculture. The Prime .Minister pointed to the fact that in years past the west has produced immense crops. That is true, and it is still capable of producing immense crops. We have a fertile soil; we have with here and there, it is true, a few exceptions, favourable weather conditions. We have an industrious population. We have men and women who for fifty years past have borne the burden and the heat of the day; they have produced immense crops, and we can produce them again. The Prime Minister, if I read correctly an account of a statement he made some time during last winter, intimated that he could not understand why with all these favourable con-22110-67
ditions there were among the fanners no reserves upon which they could fall back. I think the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) the other day clearly demonstrated why it was that there were no reserves. It is true that we have produced an immense amount of wealth, but far too small a proportion of that wealth has remained on the farm. The conditions have always been that too large a proportion of the wealth that we produce has been absorbed in its passage from the producer to the consumer. While it may be that those conditions are worse to-day than they have ever been before, nevertheless it is only the emphasis of a condition that has always prevailed. Therefore to point to the great wealth that has been produced on the prairie provinces during past years is not dealing with the situation at all.
The Prime Minister also referred to the fact that $300,000,000 were invested in automobiles and tractors. If he meant that as a further proof of the great prosperity of the west, I simply say that he has failed to take into consideration the fact that a very large proportion of that money has not yet been paid and that the farmers are still in debt for those vehicles. If he referred to that as proving that the farmers have been improvident; that they have invested where they should not have invested; that they have bought automobiles and tractors which they had no right to buy, let me say again to the Prime Minister that the privilege of using automobiles is not to be confined to the people who live in the great cities. If any class of people in the world is entitled to the use of automobiles, it is the farmer who lives out in the prairies. I might further point out that the very fact that we have spent such large sums of money on automobiles is a proof that the farmer is a good buyer and a good spender. Upon his ability to buy and spend depends the automobile industry and the living of the men who are making automobiles in this country. With regard to tractors, it is still an open question in the minds of many, and perhaps it has not yet been definitely decided whether the tractor can be used economically on the farm. Undoubtedly under certain conditions it can be. When oats were selling at 75 and 80 cents a bushel it did seem possible to save on oats and buy gasoline. But when oats are selling at 10 and 11 cents and barley at 15 cents a bushel, and gasoline still remains at the old high price, with tractors at their present high prices, and with the price likely to be still further increased if the policies of hon. gentlemen opposite prevail, it may well be questioned whether the tractor can be used economically.

Agricultural Conditions

The Prime Minister also referred to the fact, if it be a fact-I presume it is; I shall not dispute ik-that large numbers of farmers still have money in the bank. It would surely be a deplorable condition if after all these years there were no farmers with some money in the bank; but let me say that those reserves are being very rapidly depleted. Certainly nothing has been added to the bank accounts of the farmers during the last year or two. So the fact that there are still some of them with money in the bank means nothing at all. Even the farmers who do have a small current account in a bank are not necessarily solvent. It is the practice of men who wish to do business in a businesslike way to carry on their business through a bank. But money in a bank by no means proves that agriculture is solvent.
Does the Prime Minister see no significance in certain other facts? Does he see no significance in the fact that the banks have ceased to lend money to farmers? I know that that statement will be disputed, as it has been disputed by the banks; but is absolutely true that the banks will not lend money to farmers on the prospects of next year's crop. I went into a bank, not in my own town but in a neighboring town, and as I had some former acquaintance with the bank manager I had a half hour's conversation with him. I said to him, "I am not wanting to borrow any money, but I want to know if you are lending money to farmers." "Well," he said, "it depends upon circumstances. If a farmer can show good security or that he will be able to repay the loan within a little time, we will consider a loan; but if it is on the prospect of next year's crop, no." That, Mr. Speaker, is the condition which I believe is general throughout Canada. So we need not take very seriously the statements of bank managers that they are lending money to farmers. They may say so, but it is with the mental reservation that they will lend only what the farmer is entitled to. It is quite possible that neither the Prime Minister himself-nor you, Mr. Speaker, nor any of us would lend money to a man who had no prospects of repaying it. That may be good business, I am not saying that it is not; but the fact remains as it is-the banks are not lending money to farmers, and it goes to prove the statement that agriculture is practically insolvent.
Does the Prime Minister also see no significance in the fact that a limited moratorium is now in existence in each of the three prairie provinces? Surely there is some significance in that fact. Does he see no

significance in the fact that the Manitoba Debts Adjustment Act came into force only a few days ago? All these things indicate that the conditions are not as the Prime Minister described them to be. Conditions are infinitely more serious than the Prime Minister seems to think they are. Do not these facts which I have cited prove that agriculture is practically insolvent?
It is, I believe, absolutely true that the present depression has wiped out all the equity that many farmers had in their homes. It is no small thing, Mr. Speaker, for a farmer to lose the equity in his home. Remember that a farm is not merely a place of business. It is far more than that. It is the farmer's home around which many sentiments and associations have gathered for, it may be, fifty years or more, and when a farmer through force of circumstances loses the equity in his home that means infinitely more to him than it does for a business man to have to change his place of business or even to have to move from one house in the city to another. Those are the conditions that confront the farmer in this country, today, and they are conditions that cannot be minimized.
Perhaps it may not be amiss to refer to the opinions of others who are in touch with the actual conditions. The press of the west has certainly taken notice of what the Prime Minister said. I am going to quote a few extracts:
W. J. Ward of Dauphin, president of the United Farmers of Manitoba, Wednesday, spoke briefly of the statement made in the House of Commons Tuesday by Premier Bennett to the effect that the prairie provinces were not suffering undue hard times.

Mr. Ward goes on to say:
I have been a resident of the province for more than a third of a century, and have been in the closest touch especially with rural Manitoba for that entire period. For the past three or four months I have been engaged in making a tour of the province, holding meetings and discussing current conditions with the most representative farmers, merchants and others, one of my objects being to ascertain present conditions and the outlook for the future.
For Saskatchewan and Alberta I am unable to speak from personal knowledge, but so far as the province of Manitoba is concerned, I am quite able to say that Mr. Bennett does not know what he is talking about, and has not the slightest conception of the circumstances which exist here. X visited one of the rural areas of Manitoba Tuesday, not one of the worst, but one that in former years was considered among the best.
In that district I was told by the leaders, who know local conditions accurately, tint in one area ten miles square, there was but one solvent farmer left, and the country merchant is naturally, along with the farmer, in a poor position too.
I am thinking of wiring Mr. Bennett to-day, and congratulating him, so far as the west is concerned, on writing his own obituary notice. What he has said indicates a total and complete failure to appreciate a situation worse by far than was ever experienced, even in the hard early days.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, April 27, the debate on the motion of Mr. Neill for the second reading of Bill No. 8, to amend the Armistice Day Act.

maintopic: ARMISTICE DAY ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CELEBRATION OF ARMISTICE DAY ON NOVEMBER 11
speechtext: The mover of this bill has been good enough to speak to me about it on different occasions, and largely, I think, one is disposed to agree with the general idea of it. However, the bill as I read it leaves the question of Thanksgiving day pretty much as it is, and incorporates with that a day called Armistice day. The objection I have to the proposal is that the celebration or remembrance of Armistice day, if it occurs on a public holiday, is likely to lose its full significance.

maintopic: ARMISTICE DAY ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CELEBRATION OF ARMISTICE DAY ON NOVEMBER 11
speechtext: I am sure the hon. member does not wish to be unfair. It does not say a public holiday; it says legal holiday.

maintopic: ARMISTICE DAY ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CELEBRATION OF ARMISTICE DAY ON NOVEMBER 11
speechtext:
The bill reads:
Shall be a legal holiday, and shall be kept and observed as such under the name of Armistice day.

If that does not mean a public holiday, I am not sure that I know what it means or what the advantage is in declaring it a holiday at all. I am quite in accord with the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) that November 11th should be devoted primarily or exclusively, so far as the celebration goes, to a commemoration of those men who lost their lives in the war. The 11th of November is an appropriate day for that purpose. Thus far we have celebrated Armistice day on November 11 throughout the country. I cannot speak of other parts of Canada than my own home, but there, at eleven o'clock on the morning of November 11, we have a service which is attended by thousands upon thousands of people. Not only is that service attended by these thousands of people, all apparently devout, all very lovingly commemorating the men who lost their lives in the war, but at eleven o'clock, as if by common consent, throughout the whole city, in transportation activities, in industrial enterprises, in the shops, on the street, in the courts, everywhere, all activities cease for the short space of two minutes. Men go about their business afterwards but they do not lose the refreshment of memory which they have derived from that one simple act. If this day, through being made a holiday, degenerate into something that has not as its foremost and practically exclusive function this perpetuation of the memories of these men, I think we should be losing all that is sweet, all that is fine in the observances of the occasion.

maintopic: ARMISTICE DAY ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CELEBRATION OF ARMISTICE DAY ON NOVEMBER 11
speechtext:
But it has always been a
legal holiday since 1921.

maintopic: ARMISTICE DAY ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CELEBRATION OF ARMISTICE DAY ON NOVEMBER 11
speechtext:
I am not objecting to that, and the hon. member must not think I am trying to argue with him at all. My hon. friend seems disposed to make this a matter of dispute; it is not that by any manner of means. If the hon. gentleman can convince the house that this is the proper way to observe the day, well and good; I make no opposition to it. I seek only to impress upon the house what views I have of my own. I claim no special right to take part in this discussion: I do not think it is the right of one who has served any more than it is the right of anyone else. But this I do know. Perhaps some of us who have served have, more than others, just a little bit of personal recollection, a memory, whatever you may call it, that makes us feel very sincerely anxious that the day shall be observed in the proper way.
You are going to have, apparently, two holidays in the same season of the year; Thanks-

giving day is not disposed of. My fear is that this day of Armistice, this day of remembrance, as the legion has called it, will come to be just such another day as Thanksgiving is with us now. Thanksgiving day has lost its original significance, and I am not so optimistic as to suppose that, as the years and decades pass, there is going to be the same special interest in the celebration of Armistice day, or Remembrance day made into a legal holiday as there is at this moment.
Now that my hon. friend has had the opportunity of bringing this matter up again, I should have liked to have him let it lie in abeyance for a short time until all hon. members have had an opportunity of making up their minds as to whether or not we would be doing the best thing in connection with this oelebration by passing this bill. I say again, with the danger of being accused of repetition : the appreciation of what Armistice day means may disappear as the years go by and be lost, submerged and drowned in the idea of a mere public holiday. That, at all costs, I do not want to see happen, and I believe we would be encouraging that very thing by entering on a hasty disposal of this bill. Let us allow it to stand for a time. Autumn is far away and there will be time to discuss the matter in the house during this session.
I am quite sure that the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, as well as the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Gershaw), who took such an interest in the matter last year, are desirous of reaching the end I desire to reach, and that which I think it is the desire of the people of this country should be reached in connection with this proposal. The legion has written to me and I have letters from different people, some expressing one view and some another. This proposal does not altogether meet the views of the legion executive and I have written to them asking for their considered views in connection with the phase which I have presented to the house.
It is the farthest thing from my mind, and I believe it is the farthest thing from the mind of any hon. member in this house, to have this matter dealt with at arm's length. It is our idea to hold in some way a celebration which will be truly the celebration it is intended to be, one that will enable the men, women and children of this country to take from their busy lives some time in which to give a loving thought to the men we lost.

maintopic: ARMISTICE DAY ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CELEBRATION OF ARMISTICE DAY ON NOVEMBER 11
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this matter, being one of the fixing of holidays, comes under the Department of the Secretary of State, and I may say that in my capacity as such during past years
Armistice Day Act
I received considerable correspondence concerning the matter. There are two questions involved in this bill, as have been involved in similar motions which have been placed before the house at other times. One is as to whether Armistice day should be celebrated on November 11 or on the Monday of the week in which that day happens to fall, and the other is as to whether or not we should celebrate Thanksgiving day on the same day as Armistice day. Basing my opinion on the correspondence to which I have just alluded, I may say that it is my recollection and experience that the general desire of public opinion is, in the first place, to dissociate Thanksgiving day from Armistice day and, in the second place, although I have not the authority of the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary) to speak for the veterans-

maintopic: ARMISTICE DAY ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CELEBRATION OF ARMISTICE DAY ON NOVEMBER 11
speechtext:
I have no official authority
to speak for anyone.

maintopic: ARMISTICE DAY ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CELEBRATION OF ARMISTICE DAY ON NOVEMBER 11
speechtext: Then I will say "connection" or any other word that will suit my hon. friend. I meant to be complimentary to him when I said that.

maintopic: ARMISTICE DAY ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CELEBRATION OF ARMISTICE DAY ON NOVEMBER 11
speechtext: I understand that.

maintopic: ARMISTICE DAY ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CELEBRATION OF ARMISTICE DAY ON NOVEMBER 11
speechtext:
Judging from the letters
received from veterans, I should think that they would rather celebrate Armistice day on November 11, on the actual anniversary of the armistice. The reason for its being fixed on the Monday of the week in which November 11 falls was not because of the armistice, but rather to meet a situation existing in connection with Thanksgiving day. A number of representations had been received from trade and commercial institutions in favour of having Thanksgiving day celebrated on a Monday in order to give three days in which tradesmen and others could enjoy that holiday.
My reason for supporting this bill, not only as a private member but with the added experience derived from my connection with these matters, is that both difficulties may be overcome. If hon. members will read the explanatory note on the bill as printed they will find that the purpose is to repeal two sections of the act. The bill will repeal the section under which Armistice day was always celebrated on a Monday, and in that respect I think it will meet the demands of the veteran and of those most closely interested in that particular anniversary. It does away also with another section whereby the government was asked to fix Thanksgiving day on the same day as Armistice day. I think the bill meets both purposes very well, and I would commend it very strongly to the support of the house. Should this bill pass,
Armistice Day Act

Armistice day will be celebrated on November 11 and the government may fix Thanksgiving day on any other day it thinks proper, perhaps in October so as to permit a certain lapse of time between the two holidays.
The hon. member who preceded me thought that this bill might be left over for further consideration, but it is the experience of every hon. member that when public bills are not dealt with as they come before the house they are likely to be forgotten and left over for the rest of the session. This is not a new question; it was raised some two or three years ago by my hon. friend in the form of a motion, and I think every hon. member understands fully what is involved.
I repeat, as emphatically as I can, that inasmuch as we are desirous of meeting public opinion, expressed as it is by a volume of correspondence, the proper thing to do would be to adopt this bill which would permit of Armistice day being celebrated on Nevember 11, and to allow the government to fix Thanksgiving day on whatever date it chooses.

maintopic: ARMISTICE DAY ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CELEBRATION OF ARMISTICE DAY ON NOVEMBER 11
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on two previous occasions I have had the pleasure of speaking on a bill similar to this one, and I just wish to add a few words to what has already been said. A general desire has been expressed by hon. members who have spoken to have Armistice day fittingly observed; the only difference of opinion seems to be as to the exact procedure of the celebration. No one desires to see Armistice day degenerate into an ordinary public holiday, stripped of all its sad memories. Yet we must realize that almost twelve years have passed since the armistice was signed, and that a considerable number of those who took part will not have very many years more to live. Much can be done to educate school children and the younger and rising generation regarding the serious lessons of the war if Armistice day is suitably celebrated every year on the 11th of November, with the idea not of glorifying war, but rather of pointing out the sad, serious, sacred side of the war. I believe Armistice day should be observed at the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month, because it will then have that special significance which we wish it always to have.

maintopic: ARMISTICE DAY ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CELEBRATION OF ARMISTICE DAY ON NOVEMBER 11
speechtext:
May I say a word in favour of this bill? The views I wish to express are very ably set forth in a memorial which I received within the last day or two from the Canadian Legion of the British Empire Service League. This com-

munication, which is addressed to myself as a member of the house, was sent to me under date of April 24, 1931. It is as follows:
Re Observation Of Armistice Day
At a recent meeting of the Dominion executive council of the Canadian Legion of the British Empire Service League held in Ottawa, I was directed to invite your kind attention to the following resolution which was unanimously passed by the Dominion convention of the Canadian .Legion, held at Regina, Saskatchewan in November, 1929, and reaffirmed at the meeting above referred to:-
"Whereas November the eleventh is the anniversary of the cessation of hostilities in the great war and is a day sacred to all ex-service men and women and which should be sacred to the people of Canada.
And whereas the day now set apart for the observance of this anniversary does not generally coincide with the actual day.
And whereas by reason of this, the observance of this anniversary loses much of its significance, and its sacred character is thereby much impaired.
Be it therefore resolved that we request that the parliament of Canada be requested and we do hereby respectfully request it, to enact legislation whereby in place of the present Thanksgiving day, November the eleventh in every year shall be set aside as a national holiday to be known as Remembrance day."
I also wish to bring ,to the attention of the house a resolution passed by the returned men at Dauphin, Manitoba, under date of November 11, 1929. The resolution reads:
Whereas this gathering of returned men of Dauphin and district is of the opinion that the day which marked the end of hostilities in the great war should be fittingly and thankfully observed by all of the citizens of Canada in perpetuity.
And whereas we believe that the maintaining of Armistice day as a day of national import would be of inestimable value in the furtherance of ideals of peace among the nations.
And whereas in our opinion the identity of Armistice day as being the eleventh day of November is in grave danger of being lost by reason of the extent in which Armistice day has been and is being confused with Thanksgiving day in the minds of the people of Canada.
Now therefore this gathering of returned soldiers, sailors and airmen of Dauphin district, met together for the purpose of observing Armistice day, hereby records its conviction that in order that the significance of Armistice day may ever be preserved, November eleventh in each year should be set aside as a national day of observance and as a public holiday, and further that Thankgsgiving day should not be permitted in any way to detract from the memories and ideals which Armistice day should inspire in Canadians.
In accordance with the sentiments so ably and clearly set forth in these two resolutions,
I have much pleasure in supporting the bill which has been introduced by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill).

Armistice Day Act

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health

speechtext:
This bill, if it were adopted, would have the effect of making Armistice day a fixed day, the 11th of November in each year. It would be a day of observance, apart altogether from any day celebrating or commemorating any other occasion. There is in my judgment no necessity of its interfering in the slightest degree with the celebration of Thanksgiving. Coming as it does in November, it will allow ample time in October for Thanksgiving, if fixed in that month, thus avoiding the difficulties that might arise from two of these public holidays occurring within a short period of time, and more especially avoiding what I think would be an unfortunate feature, namely, that of both being celebrated on the same day. These commemorative occasions are distinct and different, and it would be unfortunate longer to try to couple the two together. Therefore I favour the passing of the bill.
What is of importance is not one's personal views, but how the proposed measure will be regarded in the country. One can judge only from personal observation, from meeting people and from general information. My view is that it will be most acceptable; that it will meet with the approval of a very large, number of people. I believe its adoption will be a source of gratification and comfort to the returned men, their families, their dependents and their descendants. I therefore support the object of this bill and strongly favour- its passage.

speechtext:
Once again, Mr. Speaker, I wish to express my approval of this proposal. On a number of occasions during the last ten years I have expressed the opinion that Armistice day and Thanksgiving day should be kept entirely separate and distinct, as they serve altogether different purposes. It does seem to me that as the years go by this country is apt to forget altogether too quickly the sacrifices made by those who had the honour and the privilege of serving overseas during the great war from 1914 to 1918. If for no other reason than that this measure is largely desired by the returned men of this country, I think that the house, in deference to them and to their request, should pass this bill. The great events of those memorable days are fading too quickly into history. We sometimes forget that England journeyed to the battlefield for one of its unknown warriors and buried him in that great sepulchre of kings and princes in the old land. Similarly the United States buried one of their unknown warriors at the national cemetery at Arlington. Italy has not been behind. From the maritime Alps they have taken an unknown warrior, and his last resting place is now by the side of that great hero and liberator of their country.
It is now some twelve years since the close of the war, and I think the question should be settled now, once and for all. The stirring deeds of those trying years are surely worth our setting aside at least one day in three hundred and sixty-five upon which to commemorate the achievements and the sacrifices not only of our own brave soldiers, but of those of our allies. It is the least we can do, and I urge upon the house that this question be settled now an in keeping with the wishes of the returned men, regardless of the feelings of the rest of the people of this country.

To my mind it is unfortunate that the proposed bill of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) attempts to make a dual change in the law as it now stands. If I correctly interpret the purport of the legislation contemplated by the bill, section 2 of the act which it is proposed to repeal originally provided that the Monday of the week in which November 11 fell should be observed ae Armistice day, and section 3 provided for the celebration of Thanksgiving day on the same day as Armistice day. By this proposed amendment you change not only the holding of both celebrations on the one day, that of remembrance and that of thanksgiving, but in addition you adopt the principle that the day of remembrance shall be the calendar day, the 1.1th of November, instead of the Monday of the week in which that day falls.
Like many hon. members of this house I have received a copy of the circular containing the resolution passed by the executive of the Dominion command of the Canadian Legion. There are many legion branches and many returned soldiers in the riding which I represent, and although it may be said that the returned men are unanimous with respect to the desirability of the observance of Armistice day as a day of remembrance separate and distinct from Thanksgiving day, there does not appear to be unanimity of opinion as to whether or not Armistice day should be observed on the Monday of the week in which the 11th of November falls or on the calendar day, the 11th of November.
I would therefore suggest, if I may, to my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni that he allow the bill to stand for a short time until we have had an opportunity of determining just what the majority of the returned men desire.

I am afraid I cannot agree with the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Lawson) in his desire to have action on the proposal of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) delayed. It has been my experience that when matters of this sort are delayed they do not further develop. So far as I am concerned I stand pledged to my comrades in the city of Regina and the province of Saskatchewan to support the eleventh of November as Armistice day, and no other day. In that part of the country the day of the week has never once entered into our discussions. Both in the local branch and in the provincial command we have taken the view that the eleventh is the eleventh, and the ninth cannot be made into the eleventh. In my locality the people interested want the eleventh and will not be satisfied with anything else.
I wish to make one or two statements in regard to the resolution passed by the Dominion command when they met in Regina. As president of the local branch it was my duty to welcome to Regina the Dominion branch. The meeting in Regina constituted the largest convention in Canada of its kind. We passed

that resolution in favour of the eleventh and never for one moment thought of any other day. I do not know what the wording is, because I have not read it, but I do remember that the eleventh of November was the day asked for by the Dominion command, a body which represents between 80,000 and 100,000 people in Canada. I suggest that we should settle this matter now, get through with it, get it out of the way and turn our minds to other business. Let us make the eleventh of November Armistice day. The members of the legion will never be content with the present arrangement. Annually the question comes up, "Why celebrate this day? It is not our day". On November 11th they visit our cenotaph and a celebration is held there and then. No matter what happens the eleventh is the day on which we hold the celebration, and the day on which we will continue to hold it.

Armistice day is the one day in the year which should be observed and commemorated more than any other. I do hope that the comments which have been made during the discussion of this bill will be kept in mind so that when it reaches the committee stage suggestions may be offered whereby the day may be fittingly observed and provision made for its proper commemoration in the future.
