That does not look as though the country were prosperous, as though there were tens of thousands of our farmers in the west with bank accounts. If they had bank accounts they would be buying. The fact that imports have fallen to the extent they have is evidence that the people are not able to buy.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Perhaps the goods are being manufactured at home.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I believe the Prime Minister himself and one or two other hon. gentlemen opposite have drawn attention to the fact that this year we have sold a great deal more wheat than we did last year. The wheat exports in the month of February of 1930 and 1931 were as follows:
1930.
1931.
Bushels
6,732,826
10,296,608
Thus it is true that in the month of February of this year we exported something over 3,500,000 bushels more than we did a year ago, but this year the wheat sold at 58 cents a bushel, whereas in I960 it sold at SI .29 a bushel. I would like to know when hon. members expect we are going to sell wheat if we cannot sell it at about 20 cents a bushel below the cost of production. It is now below the cost of production, and yet our hon. friends opposite gloat over the fact that we are selling a few bushels more this year than we did last year when wheat was worth fully double the present price.
Last year, although we exported 3,500,000 bushels less, we received $2,500,000 more than
we did the previous year. Should we keep these things quiet? Is there no connection between the figures I have quoted showing that although selling three and half million bushels more we are receiving $2,500,000 less, and the fact that our farmers are in the position in which they find themselves to-day?
There is no gainsaying the fact that the government is not making the best endeavour it can to relieve agricultural distress. If the Prime Minister would give us some favourable indication of things becoming better, he would be better employed than in lecturing us when we try to present conditions as they actually exist to our certain knowledge. I have much pleasure in seconding the amendment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have listened very attentively to the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) and the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. McKenzie), and I cannot understand them. In a time of depression they need a little more iron in their blood. The trouble with them is that they have pernicious anaemia. They are doing more harm to western Canada than ever was done to it in all the time I have lived in that part of the country. All I can call them is "calamity howlers". They are preying on the weaknesses of those who are suffering on account of lack of proper farming in western Canada and depressed prices. I want to read a clipping to show the hon. member for Assiniboia, who has just taken his seat, that there is not very much wrong in the constituency of Marquette, which is one of the most outstanding agricultural constituencies in
Agricultural Conditions

western Canada and takes second place to none. There cannot be much wrong with it. This is a clipping from the Minnedosa Tribune, under date of March 2:
Who says times are hard and money scarce? Up at the little town of Shoal Lake,-
The Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion) knows where it is, because he and I had the pleasure of addressing a meeting there.
-no less than $500 has been spent already for 1931 auto licences, as against about $40 this time last year. The amount spent in Minnedosa so far for 1931 auto licences, if you knew it, would cause you to laugh at the preacher of hard times.
That is what the Minnedosa Tribune says. Let me read this clipping from the Shoal Lake Star under date of March 26, 1931:
Payments going out by way of cream cheques have averaged around $2,500 per week, a large percentage of which has gone to the farmers of this district, the balance to outside points.
If hon. members continue to preach "blue ruin," and "hard times," they will have me feeling that I am going with them. I heard of a professor at Oxford who carried out a psychological experiment on a certain individual. About fifteen persons were to meet this man and each one was to tell him how badly he looked. This they did, and they kept it up continually until the man actually began to feel that he was ill. My hon. friends opposite will continue to cry "blue ruin" until they will have me feeling that way. I cannot stand it any longer. They are doing it for political purposes. I belong to the same organization that my hon. friend from Lisgar and my hon. friend from Assiniboia belong to-the United Farmers.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Never a very active member, though.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I was a very active member. I have sat in the organization with you. You remember quite well that in Calgary I took exception to things that you did in those organizations. You have played politics to the limit. You cannot play them any longer. You cannot work on the weakness of western people. You are political agitators.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member must address the Chair.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will admit, Mr. Speaker, that I was annoyed at the blue ruin talk that has been going on. Hon. gentlemen opposite are trying to work up political material for their associate, Mr. Ward, so that he can go round the country and talk secession and mild revolution and things of that sort. I do not wonder at the Prime Minister giving them a dressing down, for they deserve every word

of it; all he said to them was absolutely true. The hon. member for Assiniboia probably lives in a district where the men buy canned milk, where they go to the general store and buy their butter. They are not farmers. They are mostly all soil robbers, Mr. Speaker; they are causing all the trouble in western Canada.
I shall not take up any more time now; I shall defer my remarks until the budget comes before the house, when these gentlemen will probably hear more from me on the possibilities of our great west.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as
I represent a riding which is partly agricultural, I wish to take this opportunity to express my views on this subject. Since the election of July last, on every occasion that ministers or hon. members on the right addressed political banquets, they always stated that the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) had not failed in his task. The only pledge carried out, up to date, is that of the emergency session; yet the ministers contend that they have fulfilled all their pledges.
The right hon. Prime Minister, during the elections of 1930, travelled over the whole country telling the farmers:
Agriculturists, you believe in low tariff, you have been taught to applaud free trade, when did free trade fight for you? I will make protection fight for you.
Protection began in September last. I wonder how much farmers have benefited from this protection, with an increase in duties of 200 to 250 per cent on farming implements. Did this increase help the workmen? No, it favoured the manufacturers and capitalists.
The hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Sauve), in his speech, on March 26 last, stated that the Prime Minister had negotiated treaties favourable to farmers. This statement amazed me greatly-and I am not the only one among the Quebec members which it did amaze. When in the legislature, at Quebec, the hon. Postmaster General always championed the interests of the farming class, however, in his speech the other day no reference was made to farmers. He has done nothing to help them, up to this day. Like the other Conservative members of Quebec who represent agricultural ridings, he took his cue from the Prime Minister who specially favours the capitalist and manufacturer.
The hon. member for South Battleford (Mr. Vallance), on March 19 last-almost forty days ago-inquired from the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) whether he

Agricultural Conditions
had a policy to announce. The hon. minister answered that he had nothing definite so far. The minister's answer, sir, was not of a nature to encourage the farming class.
The hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Duguay) who spoke on April 13, stated that he was ready to make suggestions but that circumstances prevented him doing so because he expected the hon. Minister of Agriculture would bring down measures which would be very helpful to the farmers. In the meantime, the hon. Minister of Agriculture is conspicuous by his absence.
Assisting the farmers is an excellent way to relieve unemployment, because many of them crowd tihe cities when they can no more find their livelihood on the farm. After nine months of Conservative administration the government has not yet announced a program to assist agriculture, no.twithstanding_ all the fine pledges given by Conservative speakers who, in Quebec, insisted that they would especially help the farming class and city labour.
The workman is willing to pay a reasonable price for farm products, for when the farmer has money he is able to purchase the manufacturer's goods. The worker's motto is "live and [DOT] let live". The Conservative candidates travelled throughout Quebec, especially in the eastern townships, promising that if the Conservatives assumed office, butter imports would be prohibited. I wonder how the hon. members for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Pickel), for Stanstead (Mr. Haekett) and Compton (Mr. Gobeil), could to-day face their electors, after having promised that butter imports to this country would be prohibited? Under the Liberal regime Australia paid a duty of 1-70 cent per pound. Since the advent of the Conservative administration this duty was decreased to 1 cent, and the butter imports from Australia have been 836,000 pounds more than in 1930. I wonder whether those are the pledges or guarantees given to the electorate by the hon. members on the right.
According to the report brought down by the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), there were 6,000,000 pounds of butter imported into Canada from August 1, 1930, to March 1, 1931. As to New Zealand butter, it served its purpose in fooling the farmers, especially those of Quebec, it was stated that not a pound would enter Canada after the Conservatives assumed office, yet I find that more than 5,000,000 pounds were
imported into Canada since August 1, 1930. In 1930 we imported 408,000 pounds of butter from Australia, while in 1931, 1,244,000 pounds were imported. With these figures staring them in the face I wonder whether the hon. members on the right are fulfilling their pledges towards the electorate. It is but fair that the farmer should know what interest the government takes in his welfare.
In an answer given by the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce to a question put by the hon. member for Megantic (Mr. Roberge), the following figures were given: butter imports to Canada in November, 1930, 117,600 pounds, while in March, 1931, it was 862,904, that is seven times more than in November, 1930. Well, sir, confronted with such facts, what are we to .think of the Conservative members of Quebec who pledged themselves to protect the interests of the farmers
I fail to see what the government has done for the farmers; I fail to see what it has accomplished on behalf of the worker. However, I realize that the increases in the tariff, enacted at the emergency session, aimed at favouring the manufacturer and capitalist instead of relieving unemployment and assisting the workman and farmer.

It was not the farmer,

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not profess to have any intimate knowledge of farming conditions, but I do rise to point out to the house and to my right hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) that we have heard from his lips to-night a very different story from what we heard less than a year ago. I do not know that I have ever heard a more vehement lecture to hon. members in this house than was delivered to-night by my right hon. friend concerning the matter of talking blue ruin and running down the credit of the country. I rise simply in order that he and the people may not forget some of the statements made by him within the last year with regard to the country whose credit he now desires to be upheld, concerning existing conditions as he described them throughout the country. These
Agricultural Conditions

statements to which I shall refer were made at a time when he was not averse to running down the country or crying blue ruin, and at a time when on every platform he seemed to have one desire at least, and that was to let not only this country but the world at large know exactly how badly oil we were.
I shall quote to the house some of the expression used by my right hon. friend during the election campaign with regard to conditions in this country, and then let us see if this is the same gentleman who to-night has condemned everybody who has attempted to tell the truth with regard to conditions as they exist in Canada to-day. Speaking at Toronto he said:
To-day we have unemployment on a scale never before known.
Speaking at Inverness he said:
Canada's national resources are being depleted.
Again speaking at Toronto he said:
Canadian industries are dying.
Speaking of trade generally, he said:
Thus Canada is becoming more and more a dependent, and less and less independent economically. . . .

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is true.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Ottawa Citizen carried the statement from him that "industry was languishing:" Speaking at Regina, he said:
Now we have unemployment, people walking our streets, men and women hungry,-we have all these things in this great rich country.
Speaking of the then Prime Minister he said:
How ever blind he may be to your future, and deaf to your present needs, surely he cannot stop his ears with smug complacence and self esteem to the cry that carries across the nation, the cry of the destitute and hungry, the cry of mothers and fathers and little children who call to us as Christians and as Canadians to heal their pain.
And he spoke of "this time of national distress."

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Those are statements made at that time by my right hon. friend in regard to conditions in this country. Speaking of the west, as reported in a speech at Winnipeg:
After stressing the economic ills of western Canada, showing that the prairies could not sell "wheat, foodstuffs, cattle and dairy products" ....

I ask hon. members if there could be any statements which would be less likely to obtain credit for the farmers than a statement of that kind made on a platform by the hon. gentleman who to-night condemned anybody who attempts to say that the farmer is not at the present time in a prosperous condition. Speaking at Sydney he said:
Now my fellow Canadians are out of a job, children hungry, mothers hungry, men willing to work but unable to get work ....
Those are pictures which were painted last July by my right hon. friend. While it may be good politics for him to rise in his place at this time and lecture hon. gentlemen for having dared to come here and state conditions as they exist, I do not believe it add3 anything to the debate, or that the country will be at all misled by the attitude which he takes.
He endeavours to salve his conscience, if I may use that term without disrespect, by saying that he has faith in this country. I want to state to him that he has not a monopoly on faith. All of us believe in the future of Canada, but we believe that its highest development in the future can best be attained by knowing all the conditions which require attention at any particular period land by endeavouring to remedy those conditions. Particularly I would call upon my right hon. friend, who was so lavish in his promises, to bring out his remedy and have the changes brought about. To-night my right hon. friend, amid loud cheers and applause from his followers, said that given health and strength and a term of office he would bring this country through its difficulties. May I say to my right hon. friend that there is always a time when a note falls due, and he already has had nine months in which to fulfil his promises. Considering the conditions which have been pointed out and which are said to exist in this country one would not be led to think that so far he had been very successful in his efforts; and one can be excused if he has considerable doubt as to whether the term of office for which he asks will be very fruitful of results. He is no doubt entitled to a reasonable time to bring about changes, but he must remember that the promises he made when he painted these conditions were promises for immediate action, and there was no suggestion that we would have to await the turn of a cycle of depression and for economic readjustment; the change was going to be made out of the air and in some way entirely unknown to those who were not "in the secret" when he

Agricultural Conditions
sat on this side of the house he refused to disclose to this house and country what his policy was. He said, "I am like the great statesmen in England; when I am called in, then I will prescribe." He has been called in, and for nine months he has had the opportunity of prescribing. We know how this country really stands at the present time, and I do not think that so far he can look with a great deal of pride upon the patient he has been attending.
To-night, referring to the statements made by my hon. friend from Lisgar (Mr. Brown) the Prime Minister said "What good on earth can come from such statements as these?" Those words might well have been used at a time when he was travelling throughout the length and breadth of this land. The answer he would probably have made in private would have been, "At least it may do this; it may assist me and my party to get into power." They had that effect, and he is in power. He has the opportunity and the responsibility. I say to him that hon. members on this side of the house, and I think on the other side, notwithstanding the scolding, will continue to present to him conditions as they exist in various constituencies so that he may apply the remedies which he says he has. It is to be hoped that they will not continue to be met with lectures or with the suggestion he makes that a man who presents difficulties is not true to his country. Loyalty to our country is in all of us. Faith in our country and in its resources is in all of us. At the same time we cannot make that faith known and effective, and cannot make our country grow unless we have before us the true state of conditions. There is no use of my right hon. friend figuratively putting his head in the sand and refusing to see conditions as they are. He knows what they are as well as anybody else, and my right hon. friend may as well make up his mind to it that he will be held to his pledges, to remedy those conditions in order that the new era of which he talked and the promises he made may materialize.
As I say, I do not propose, nor do I feel qualified, to make any extended contribution to the debate in regard to agricultural conditions. But with all deference to my right hon. friend I submit that he himself made no contribution in this particular; rather he attempted to draw a red herring across the trail by blaming hon. gentlemen on this side for referring to the conditions existing in their several constituencies. I rose, Mr. Speaker, only for the purpose of reminding my right hon. friend of the attitude he took not very long ago, and of assuring him that we will
continue to present the situation as it really is, regardless of whether he approves or disapproves of that course.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been listening very attentively to this discussion on agriculture. I noticed that the speeches bore mostly on conditions existing in the west, such as the sale price of wheat and the financial difficulties of many western farmers. The west is not the only place where there are farmers and where farming suffers from present conditions. I have the privilege of representing a Tiding where there are a large number of farmers as well as industrialists, manufacturers and merchants, and iit is on their behalf that I wish to point out to the house what the farming community of Terrebonne thinks of the present agricultural situation. The farmers of my riding suffer like all farmers in this country from the failure to sell their products and the greatly decreased prices offered for them.
The present government, on many occasions during the last elections made pledges as regards this situation. Many pledges, but nothing has been done so far. I shall quote, among many, the pledges made by the hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) as reported by the Ottawa Journal on July 2, 1930:
I state that I shall regard as my great responsibility if elected on July 28, to see that the collective weight and power of the Dominion of Canada is placed behind agriculture.
I would be lacking in qualification entitling me to head a government if I failed to do so.
Speaking in Quebec, according to the Ottawa Citizen, on July 14, he stated:
I do not want place and power over broken promises.
Well, I wonder what the government has done to help agriculture? I have no idea. I am not aware of any measure introduced in the house this session or at the September session, which would improve the farming situation. In the statements made by members of the government, I find nothing relating to agriculture. May I quote certain extracts from a speech delivered by the hon. Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau) and reported by the newspaper La Presse, on February 23. In this speech delivered before the Conservative Women's Association, of Montreal, the hon. minister spoke quite at length on the pledges made by the right hon. Mr. Bennett, when he took office, and the way in which he had fulfilled those pledges, he then added:
The pledge to increase the duties on about 200 articles which flood the local market to

the detriment of the manufacturer and Canadian farmer was carried out at the emergency session. What was the result? The factories of Quebec, to mention these only, are undertaking millions of dollars worth of development. A market valued at $32,000,000 is opened to the cotton manufacturers; one of $42,000,000 for woollens and another of $13,000,000 for silk goods.
Is there, sir, in this extract one word to help the farmers? No. The finst act of the government was to favour the manufacturers and industrialists. I have no objection to the government favouring to a certain extent important industrial groups, however, I state that agriculture should have preference. Both classes might have been simultaneously favoured by the government. I shall equally quote the words of another minister who seemed to reflect the views of the present government. The speech was made by the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Sauve) on March 23, at a meeting of the Conservative Women's Association of Montreal. . . .
